newsitem.title: FRANCE: French poll axe hits rightist sleaze probe targets.
newsitem.headline: French poll axe hits rightist sleaze probe targets.

text.p: A handful of rightist politicians touched by corruption probes got their comeuppance at the hands of voters in the French general election, but others surprisingly kept their seats and claimed vindication.
Sleaze was a major issue in the election campaign, but it cut unevenly, leaving all tainted left-wing candidates unscathed, final official results showed on Monday.
Conservative President Jacques Chirac dissolved parliament nearly 10 months ahead of schedule, hoping to renew his rightist majority but the poll ended instead in an upset leftist victory.

During the campaign leftist candidates accused the right of plotting to protect targets of corruption probes by granting them amnesty after the election, ironically a step taken most recently by a leftist parliament in 1990.
The right flatly denied the accusation but it nonetheless clearly hurt the government campaign.
Reflecting the national result, rightists tainted by corruption allegations took the brunt of voters' anger while leftists linked to possible wrongdoing fared better.
The highest-ranking member of Chirac's Gaullist party to lose in Sunday's election was Justice Minister Jacques Toubon.
While not himself a target of corruption probes, Toubon was accused by the Socialists of blocking or burying judicial inquiries involving other Gaullists.

In one highly publicised incident, his ministry chartered a helicopter last year to try to track down a state prosecutor trekking in Nepal in a bungled attempt to head off a probe of Gaullist Paris mayor Jean Tiberi, about to be launched by the prosecutor's independent-minded deputy.
Tiberi himself survived Sunday's vote in his Paris district and promptly claimed voters had recognised his integrity despite the "unspeakable calumnies" to which he had been subjected.
Not so lucky was centrist former industry ministry Gerard Longuet, forced out of the cabinet of ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur in 1995 due to a sleaze probe.

Defeated in the May 25 first-round vote was Isabelle Balkany, wife of former Gaullist parliamentarian Patrick Balkany, who had himself been barred from standing again due to an earlier corruption conviction.
However, several other rightists and leftists snarled in sleaze probes managed to win re-election along with Tiberi.
Among them were Gaullist deputy Frank Marlin, former Socialist Party leader Henri Emmanuelli, Communist Party chief Robert Hue and Socialist ex-prime minister Laurent Fabius.

Fabius came under investigation in connection with the 1980s distribution, at a time when he was prime minister, of AIDS-tainted blood products which killed hundreds of haemophiliacs. Now he has been re-elected, he is expected to become speaker of the new, leftist-dominated National Assembly.

Emmanuelli, who was given a one-year suspended sentence for his role in allegedly improper fundraising activities, is said not to be in line for a post in the new government being formed by Lionel Jospin, the austere Socialist Prime Minister-designate.
Hue, who is under investigation for alleged ties to illicit Communist fundraising, could provide an early test of Jospin's ethics policies.
Jospin has pledged to continue a centre-right policy of barring anyone from government who is formally under investigation in connection with official sleaze.
